questions.q: A novel's hero is a clerk crushed by a bureaucracy he can't understand, and we watch him with pity from above. Which of Frye's modes is this?
choices: High mimetic
Low mimetic
Romantic
Ironic
questions.explain: In the ironic mode the hero is inferior to us in power or intelligence, so we look down on a scene of frustration or absurdity.

questions.q: A screenwriter's story ends with a young couple's wedding, the disapproving father finally joining the feast. Which mythos, and which season?
choices: Comedy, the mythos of spring
Romance, the mythos of summer
Tragedy, the mythos of autumn
Irony, the mythos of winter
questions.explain: Frye's comedy forms a new society around the young hero and tends to convert blocking characters rather than expel them.

questions.q: What decides a work's mode, for Frye?
choices: The number of acts and their order
The hero's power of action relative to us and to their world
Whether it ends in marriage or death
The historian's choice of plot for the facts
questions.explain: The modes run from mythic (a god) to ironic (weaker than us). The last option is Hayden White's use of Frye's mythoi.

questions.q: In As You Like It, the exiled characters flee to the Forest of Arden, are changed there, and return to renew the court. What did Frye call such a place?
choices: The special world
The inmost cave
The green world
Base reality
questions.explain: Frye's green world, from "The Argument of Comedy" (1948). The special world and inmost cave are Vogler's; base reality is improv's.

questions.q: How does Frye arrange his four mythoi?
choices: In a line from beginning to end, like acts
On a circle of seasons, with comedy opposite tragedy and romance opposite irony, each shading into its neighbours
As seven plots driven by the ego and the Self
As thirty-six situations defined by their roles
questions.explain: The seasonal circle lets each mythos blend into the next. The others are Booker's and Polti's systems.

questions.q: A journalist realizes she has written a reformer's story as a quest with a triumphant hero, when the same facts could show a system swallowing good intentions. Whose borrowing of Frye is she applying?
choices: Hayden White's: the same facts can be emplotted as romance or irony
Aristotle's: plot is the soul of tragedy
Booker's: the monster is the ego
Polti's: a situation is defined by its roles
questions.explain: White took Frye's four mythoi into history-writing, arguing the choice of plot is not dictated by the evidence.

questions.q: What's the most common criticism of Frye's system?
choices: That it only covers comedy
That it ranks works too harshly
That it relies on box-office data
That it's too schematic and ahistorical, floating free of who wrote and why
questions.explain: Critics from W. K. Wimsatt to Fredric Jameson found it too tidy and too detached from history; Frye in fact tried to keep value judgments out.

ideas: All stories move through four basic plots tied to the seasons: comedy is spring, romance summer, tragedy autumn, irony and satire winter.
Fiction can be sorted by the hero's power of action relative to us, from gods down to figures weaker than ourselves.
European fiction has moved steadily down from gods to heroes to ordinary people to the trapped and absurd.
In comedy's green world, characters escape a harsh society, are transformed, and return to renew it.
